title: Homestay Listing Optimisation: Airbnb, Booking.com, MakeMyTrip
excerpt: How to improve a homestay listing on Airbnb, Booking.com and MakeMyTrip: photo order, titles, house rules, calendar sync, replies and seasonal pricing.
description: Optimise homestay listings on Airbnb, Booking.com and MakeMyTrip: photos, titles, house rules, calendar sync, response rate and seasonal pricing.
html:
To get more bookings from Airbnb, Booking.com and MakeMyTrip, a homestay should lead with its strongest photo, write a title and description that say exactly what the stay offers, set clear house rules, sync calendars to prevent double bookings, reply to enquiries quickly, and adjust prices for season, weekends and length of stay.

Why the same homestay performs differently on each OTA

Each platform shows your property to a different kind of traveller in a different way. Airbnb leans on photos, host profile and reviews, and guests often message before booking. Booking.com and Agoda are used by many international and business travellers who filter hard on facilities and cancellation terms. MakeMyTrip and Goibibo are where a large share of domestic leisure travellers compare prices and offers. The listing basics are the same everywhere, but you should check each one as a guest would on a phone, because that is how most people see it.

OTAs are a strong source of first-time guests. The aim of a good listing is to convert those views into bookings and good reviews, and then to bring satisfied guests back directly, as described in our post on B&B direct bookings without a booking engine.

Photos: what to shoot and in what order

The first photo decides whether someone taps on your listing in a search result. The next four or five decide whether they keep scrolling.

  1. Hero photo: the single thing guests will remember, such as the view from the balcony in Munnar, the estate bungalow in Coorg or the wooden house in Sikkim. Daylight, straight horizon, no people blocking it.
  2. Best room: a wide shot from the doorway corner, bed made, curtains open.
  3. Bathroom: clean, well lit, showing geyser and fittings. Guests worry about bathrooms more than anything else.
  4. Common space: sit-out, dining room or garden where guests will actually spend time.
  5. Food: a real breakfast you serve, not a stock image.
  6. Surroundings: the walk, the stream, the tea garden, the village.
  7. Every other room type, each labelled correctly so guests see exactly what they are booking.
  8. Practical shots: parking, the approach road, the signboard, power backup if you have it.

Shoot on a recent phone in daylight, hold it level and at chest height, and avoid heavy filters. If a room looks smaller than in the photos, the guest will say so in the review. For more on visual content, see our guide to resort photography and video.

Titles and descriptions that answer the guest's questions

Titles

Where a platform lets you write your own title, use it for the two or three facts that set you apart: the setting, the type of stay and one strong feature. For example, "Coffee estate homestay with valley view, home-cooked Kodava meals" says more than "Luxury stay in Coorg". Avoid capital letters, symbols and claims like "best" that guests do not believe.

Descriptions

Structure the description so a guest can scan it on a phone:

  • One opening line on what the stay feels like and who it suits (couples, families, groups of friends, remote workers).
  • The rooms: beds, bathrooms, maximum guests, balcony or view.
  • Food: what is included, what is extra, whether you can cater to Jain, vegetarian or non-vegetarian preferences.
  • Location: distance and travel time to the nearest town, station and key sights, and whether the last stretch is a rough road.
  • The host: who lives on the property and how guests can reach you.
  • Honest limitations: patchy mobile signal, steps, no lift, power cuts in monsoon.

Fill in every amenity and facility field too. Guests filter by them, and a missing tick for "parking" or "pets allowed" can hide you from the very search you suit.

House rules and policies that prevent bad reviews

Most bad reviews at homestays come from mismatched expectations, not bad service. Write rules that are short and specific:

  • Check-in and check-out times, and whether late arrivals are possible.
  • Quiet hours, music and alcohol policy, especially for groups.
  • Pets, smoking, outside visitors and unmarried couples policy, stated plainly if you have one.
  • ID requirements at check-in.
  • Extra guests, children's age bands and extra-bed charges.

Choose a cancellation policy on each platform that you can live with. Stricter policies protect peak dates; more flexible ones can make your listing more attractive in quieter months. Many owners use different policies for different seasons where the platform allows it.

Calendar sync and avoiding double bookings

A double booking is one of the fastest ways to damage your standing on a platform and with a guest. If you list on more than one OTA and also take direct bookings, choose one of these approaches:

ApproachHow it worksSuits
Manual blockingUpdate every extranet by hand after each booking, from one master calendarOne to three rooms, one or two OTAs
iCal syncPlatforms that support it export and import calendar links so blocked dates copy acrossSmall properties on Airbnb plus one or two others
Channel managerSoftware that updates rates and inventory across connected OTAs togetherMore rooms, more channels, frequent bookings

iCal sync is not instant, so a booking can still slip through in the gap. Whichever method you use, check your master calendar every morning and right after every booking.

Response rate and guest messages

Platforms track how quickly and how often you reply to enquiries and booking requests, and slow replies can count against you. Turn on notifications in each host app on a phone that someone always carries. Save reply templates for common questions (how to reach, food, children, parking), and personalise the first line. If you cannot accept a request, decline it politely rather than letting it expire.

Pricing by season, weekend and length of stay

A single flat rate all year leaves money on the table in peak season and leaves rooms empty in quiet months. Set up a simple pricing calendar:

  • Peak dates: long weekends, Diwali, Christmas to New Year, summer holidays for hill stations, and local festivals such as Onam or Dussehra where relevant.
  • Weekends versus weekdays: many properties near Bengaluru, Pune or Delhi see demand bunch on Friday and Saturday nights.
  • Monsoon and off-season: lower rates or added value, such as an included meal, to attract weekday and long-stay guests.
  • Length-of-stay discounts: weekly or longer-stay discounts where the platform offers them, which suit remote workers and families.
  • Minimum stay: two-night minimums on peak weekends stop single nights from blocking longer bookings.

Keep your rates consistent with your contracts. In October 2022 the Competition Commission of India fined MakeMyTrip-Goibibo and directed it to drop "wide" price and room parity obligations relative to other OTAs, while treating "narrow" parity covering the property's own website as potentially justifiable. Agreements differ, so read your own.

Frequently asked questions

Which OTA is best for a small homestay in India?

It depends on who your guests are. Airbnb suits properties with a strong host story and unique setting. MakeMyTrip and Goibibo reach many domestic leisure travellers. Booking.com and Agoda bring more international guests. Start with the one or two that match your guests, run them well, and add more only when you can keep every calendar accurate.

How do I stop double bookings across Airbnb and Booking.com?

Keep one master calendar and block dates everywhere as soon as a booking is confirmed. Where both platforms support iCal calendar links, connect them so blocked dates copy across, but remember the sync has a delay and check after every booking. If you have several rooms and several channels, a channel manager that updates inventory together is the safer option.

How often should I change my listing photos?

Update them whenever something changes, such as a renovated room, new furniture or a new view after landscaping, and review the full set at least once a year. Seasonal photos, like monsoon greenery or a winter bonfire, can be moved to the front at the right time. Remove any photo that no longer matches what guests will find.

Should I give discounts for longer stays?

Often, yes. Longer stays mean fewer check-ins, less cleaning and fewer empty nights between bookings. Weekly or monthly discounts can attract remote workers, families on long holidays and retired travellers, especially in the off-season. Set the discount so the total still covers your costs, and use minimum-stay rules on peak weekends instead.

Where to start

Open your listing on each platform on a phone, as a guest would. Reorder the photos so the hero shot and bathroom come first, rewrite the description using the checklist above, and set up a master calendar with sync or manual blocking. Then mark peak dates and set weekend and length-of-stay pricing for the next six months. For broader help across channels, see our hospitality page.
